message.content:
**Hydrogen – A Quick Reference Guide to Its Properties**

| Category | Property | Value / Description | Notes |
|----------|----------|---------------------|-------|
| **Basic Atomic Data** | Atomic number | 1 | Only one proton in the nucleus. |
| | Atomic mass (average) | 1.008 u | Weighted average of natural isotopes. |
| | Electron configuration | 1s¹ | One valence electron. |
| | Ionization energy (1st) | 13.598 eV | Highest among all elements. |
| | Electron affinity | –0.754 eV | Smallest among the elements. |
| | Electronegativity (Pauling) | 2.20 | Highest of all elements. |
| | Atomic radius (covalent) | 31 pm | Very small due to single electron. |
| | Van der Waals radius | 120 pm | For H₂ molecules. |
| | Nuclear spin | ½ (¹H) | ¹H has nuclear spin ½; ²H has 1; ³H has ½. |
| | Magnetic moment | 2.792847 µ_N | For ¹H nucleus. |
| | Isotopes | ¹H (protium), ²H (deuterium), ³H (tritium) | ¹H ~99.98 %, ²H ~0.02 %, ³H trace. |
| | Half‑life (³H) | 12.32 years | Radioactive β⁻ emitter. |
| **Physical State (STP)** | State | Gas | Diatomic H₂. |
| | Boiling point | –252.87 °C (20.28 K) | Extremely low. |
| | Melting point | –259.16 °C (14.01 K) | Extremely low. |
| | Density (gas, STP) | 0.08988 g L⁻¹ | Lightest gas. |
| | Density (liquid, 20 K) | 0.0708 g cm⁻³ | Lower than water. |
| | Molar volume (gas, STP) | 22.414 L mol⁻¹ | Standard value. |
| | Molar mass | 2.01588 g mol⁻¹ (H₂) | 1.00794 g mol⁻¹ per atom. |
| | Specific heat (gas, 25 °C) | 28.836 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹ | High due to light mass. |
| | Thermal conductivity (gas, 25 °C) | 0.180 W m⁻¹ K⁻¹ | Highest among gases. |
| | Speed of sound (gas, 25 °C) | 1270 m s⁻¹ | Fastest in air. |
| | Refractive index (gas, 589 nm) | 1.000132 | Very close to unity. |
| | Dielectric constant (gas) | 1.000132 | Same as refractive index. |
| | Viscosity (gas, 25 °C) | 1.628 µPa s | Low viscosity. |
| | Surface tension (liquid, 20 K) | 0.0001 N m⁻¹ | Very low. |
| | Vapor pressure (liquid, 20 K) | 1 atm | By definition. |
| **Chemical Properties** | Bond type | Diatomic covalent (H–H) | Single σ bond. |
| | Bond dissociation energy | 436 kJ mol⁻¹ | Strong bond. |
| | Oxidation states | +1, –1 | Forms H⁺ (proton) and hydride H⁻. |
| | Acidic behavior | Strong acid (H⁺) | In aqueous solution, forms hydronium. |
| | Basic behavior | Weak base (H⁻) | Hydride ion is a strong base. |
| | Redox potential (H⁺/H₂) | 0 V (standard hydrogen electrode) | Reference electrode. |
| | Flammability | Extremely flammable | Combustion: 2 H₂ + O₂ → 2 H₂O. |
| | Combustion enthalpy | –285.83 kJ mol⁻¹ (per H₂O) | Exothermic. |
| | Solubility in water | 0.0006 g g⁻¹ (at 25 °C) | Very low. |
| | Solubility in organic solvents | High | Dissolves in many nonpolar solvents. |
| | Hydrogen bonding | Weak (H₂ does not form H‑bond) | But H⁺ can form strong H‑bonds. |
| | Isotope effects | Kinetic isotope effect (H/D) | Deuterium reacts slower (~2×). |
| | Spectroscopic features | Rotational spectrum (microwave) | Sharp lines at ~2.1 THz. |
| | Nuclear magnetic resonance | ¹H NMR (proton) | 100 MHz for ¹H at 9.4 T. |
| | UV‑Vis absorption | None (diatomic H₂ is homonuclear) | Requires electronic transition. |
| | Infrared absorption | None (H₂ is homonuclear) | Requires dipole change. |
| **Isotopic Variants** | ¹H (protium) | Stable | Most abundant. |
| | ²H (deuterium) | Stable | 1 in 6000 atoms. |
| | ³H (tritium) | Radioactive | β⁻ emitter, half‑life 12.32 yr. |
| | Chemical differences | Deuterium forms stronger bonds (bond strength ↑) | Leads to kinetic isotope effect. |
| | Physical differences | Deuterium melts at 18.67 K, boils at 23.71 K | Slightly heavier. |
| | Applications | Tritium used in nuclear fusion, radiolabeling | Deuterium used in D‑T fusion, heavy water. |
| **Astrophysical & Cosmological** | Abundance in Universe | ~75 % by mass | Most abundant element. |
| | Role in stars | Fusion: 4 H → He (proton‑proton chain, CNO cycle) | Energy source of Sun. |
| | Spectral lines | Lyman series (UV) | 121.6 nm (Ly‑α). |
| | Interstellar medium | H I (neutral), H₂ (molecular clouds) | Traced by 21 cm line. |
| | Cosmological significance | First element formed in Big Bang nucleosynthesis | Provides constraints on cosmology. |
| **Industrial & Practical** | Production | Steam reforming of hydrocarbons, electrolysis of water | Large scale. |
| | Storage | Compressed gas, cryogenic liquid, metal hydrides | Safety considerations. |
| | Uses | Fuel (hydrogen fuel cells), feedstock (ammonia, methanol), metallurgy | Clean energy potential. |
| | Safety | Explosive limits: 4–75 % in air | Requires ventilation, leak detection. |
| | Environmental impact | Zero CO₂ when burned | Emits water vapor; still requires renewable electricity for green H₂. |

---

### Quick Takeaways

1. **Lightest Element** – Hydrogen is the simplest and lightest element, with a single proton and one electron.
2. **Strongest Electronegativity** – It pulls electrons most strongly, making it a powerful acid (H⁺) and a weak base (H⁻).
3. **Flammability & Energy** – Combustion releases a lot of energy per gram, but the reaction is highly exothermic and requires careful handling.
4. **Isotopic Diversity** – Deuterium and tritium introduce subtle but important differences in chemistry and physics, especially in nuclear fusion research.
5. **Cosmic Dominance** – Hydrogen fuels stars and dominates the mass of the universe, making it central to astrophysics and cosmology.

Feel free to ask for deeper dives into any of these categories—whether you want the quantum mechanical details of the H₂ molecule, the thermodynamics of hydrogen storage, or the role of hydrogen in stellar nucleosynthesis!
